Your first speaking session: how to start without an audience

Your first speaking session does not need an audience or perfect grammar. Here is a small loop you can do alone, today, in about 15 minutes.

Published April 12, 2024 · 6 min read · Sławomir Onyszko ·Updated November 8, 2026

It is easy to wait to feel ready before you speak a new language. You finish another course, learn more words, or look for a patient person who will not judge you. The wait can last years.

Speaking is not a test you pass once you know enough. It is a skill you build by doing it. The first session does not need an audience, a perfect accent, or a long conversation. It needs a prompt, your voice, and a correction.

Why waiting feels safer than speaking

When you read or listen, you can stay in control. You recognize words and understand the meaning. Nothing embarrassing happens. When you speak, you hear your own voice, you pause, and you make mistakes in front of yourself. That feels exposed, even when nobody else is listening.

Recognition and production are different skills. Production means building your own sentence and saying it out loud. You can understand a sentence when someone else says it and still freeze when you have to build it. Reading about swimming will not teach you to swim. At some point you have to get in the water.

I know this feeling. For years I understood more than I could say. My first real attempt at speaking was a short recording I made alone in my room. It was awkward. It was also the first time I heard the gap between what I knew and what I could produce.

What the first session actually needs

Three things:

  • a prompt that gives you something to say
  • your voice, recorded or spoken aloud
  • a correction you can understand

Everything else is optional. You do not need a tutor, a language exchange partner, or a perfect study plan. Those can help later. For the first session, you need one short answer and a look at what happened.

A 15-minute first session

  1. Read a short story at your level. Choose something you understand without translating every word.
  2. Answer one speaking task. It can be a description of yourself, your day, or a picture.
  3. Record your answer. Do not correct yourself while you speak. The point is to hear what you actually say.
  4. Compare your version with the correction. Read the explanation and check that you understand the difference.
  5. Save one correction as a flashcard. Do not save all of them, just the one that seems most important.

The story gives you words and context. The speaking task asks you to use them. The correction shows you a more natural version. The flashcard brings the correction back later.

Suppose the task asks you to describe yourself. You say: "I have 30 years and I live in Krakow." The correction says: "I am 30 years old and I live in Krakow." The explanation is simple: English uses "be" for age, not "have". You save that correction. A few days later, the app asks you to use "I am ... years old" again.

What to do when you freeze

When you freeze, lower the difficulty. Describe what you see in the room. Say three sentences about your day. Use the words from the story even if the grammar is rough. A short, imperfect answer is better than a perfect answer you never record.

If you have no words, describe the thing around the missing word. "The thing you use to cut bread" is a useful answer if you do not know "knife". The correction will give you the word. That is how the gap closes.

What a useful correction looks like

A useful correction tells you three things:

  • what you said
  • what a more natural version is
  • why the change matters

"I have 30 years" is not a random mistake. It is a pattern from your first language. When the correction explains the pattern, you can fix more than one sentence.

A correction that only says "wrong" is not enough. You need the reason, or you will repeat the same pattern.

Why practicing alone works

Practicing alone works because it removes the social cost. You can pause, repeat, and make the same mistake ten times without worrying about someone's patience. You can record a sentence until it feels less awkward. You can do it at 7 in the morning or 11 at night.

A tutor is still the gold standard for real conversation. A tutor can interrupt, ask follow-up questions, and react to what you say. That is hard to replace. But you do not need a tutor for your first session. You need one small loop you can repeat until speaking feels less foreign.

What not to do in the first week

  • Do not wait for a perfect accent. Accent is part of who you are. The goal is to be understood, not to sound like someone else.
  • Do not memorize a speech. A memorized speech can sound good and still leave you frozen when the question changes.
  • Do not collect apps and books as a substitute for speaking. A new resource feels productive. It is still not production.
  • Do not learn a list of words without using them. A word you recognize is not yet a word you can say.

A simple first week

  • Day 1: Set up a session and answer one speaking task. Save one correction.
  • Day 2: Do another short session. Repeat the same task if you want.
  • Day 3: Review the correction from day 1. Say the corrected sentence out loud.
  • Day 4: Read a new story and answer one task.
  • Day 5: Review your corrections. Pick one pattern to watch.
  • Day 6: Do a longer answer, about five sentences.
  • Day 7: Look back at your corrections. Notice one thing that got easier.

If you miss a day, continue on the next day. The plan is a suggestion, not a streak you have to protect.

Hard questions

Do I need a tutor to start?

No. A tutor is the best place to practice real conversation, but you can build your first speaking habit alone. A tutor becomes more useful when you can already produce a few sentences and want to work on spontaneity.

What if I make mistakes?

Mistakes are the material. A correction you understand is more useful than a perfect sentence you copied.

How long should a session take?

Ten to fifteen minutes is enough for a first session. On a busy day, five minutes with one speaking task and one review still counts.

What if I do not know enough words?

Use simple words and describe around the missing one. The correction will give you the word you needed. Over time, your sentences will grow.

Start with one answer

The first session is not supposed to be impressive. It is supposed to happen. One answer, one correction, one review. That is the loop.
